content: 1. All adult and adolescent women from key populations who are living with HIV and are pregnant should receive appropriate HIV treatment and care, in accordance with WHO guidelines, to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV. 2. Many women from key populations, particularly adolescents, have inadequate access to antenatal care, often attend late in pregnancy, and have limited access to prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services. 3. Young women, like all women, should be counseled about the permanency of sterilization and the availability of alternative, long-term, highly effective contraceptive methods. Studies indicate that up to 20% of women sterilized at a young age later regret this decision, with young age being a strong predictor of regret and requests for reversal. 4. Young men, like all men, should be counseled about the permanency of sterilization and the availability of alternative, long-term, highly effective contraceptive methods. Evidence shows that men who undergo vasectomy at younger ages are more likely to seek reversal compared to those who undergo the procedure at older ages. 5. Young women (from menarche to under 18 years) can generally use depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) as a contraceptive method (MEC category 2). 6. Combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) may decrease bone mineral density (BMD) in adolescents, especially those using very low-dose formulations (<30 µg ethinyl estradiol-containing combined oral contraceptives). However, CHC use has little to no effect on BMD in premenopausal women. 7. Scientifically accurate and comprehensive sexuality education programs, both within and outside schools, should include information on contraceptive use and acquisition. 8. Financial barriers to contraceptive use should be eliminated for marginalized populations, including adolescents and the poor, to make contraceptives affordable and accessible to all. 9. Safe abortion information and services should be provided in accordance with existing WHO guidelines to ensure safety and accessibility. 10. Sexual and reproductive health services, including contraceptive information and services, should be made available to adolescents without mandatory parental or guardian authorization to meet their educational and service needs. 11. Skills-based, interactive, and participatory approaches, including online, mobile health, peer, and outreach methods, have shown promise in reducing the risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and HIV among adolescents from key populations. 12. Brief sexuality-related communication (BSC) is recommended in primary health services to prevent sexually transmitted infections among adults and adolescents. 13. Women younger than 30 years should not undergo cervical cancer screening unless they are known to be HIV-infected or living in areas with high HIV prevalence. 14. Children and young people aged 5–17 years should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily. Activities exceeding 60 minutes daily provide additional health benefits, and most of the activity should be aerobic, with vigorous-intensity activities, including muscleand bone-strengthening exercises, incorporated at least three times per week. 15. Adults aged 18–64 years should perform at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity per week, or at least 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity, or an equivalent combination. For additional health benefits, adults should increase moderate-intensity activity to 300 minutes per week or engage in 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity. Muscle-strengthening activities involving major muscle groups should be done on two or more days per week. 16. School-based life skills education should be encouraged to promote mental health in children and adolescents, where feasible. 17. Suicide prevention programs in school settings, including mental health awareness and skills training, can be implemented to reduce suicide attempts and deaths among adolescent students. 18. WHO recommends reducing free sugar intake to less than 10% of total energy intake for both adults and children, with a further reduction to below 5% suggested for additional health benefits. 19. WHO recommends increasing potassium intake from food to reduce blood pressure and the risk of cardiovascular disease, stroke, and coronary heart disease. For adults, a potassium intake of at least 90 mmol/day (3510 mg/day) is suggested, with adjustments for children based on their energy requirements. 20. Routine use of multiple micronutrient powders during pregnancy is not recommended as an alternative to standard iron and folic acid supplementation for improving maternal and infant health outcomes. 21. Vitamin A supplementation in postpartum women is not recommended for preventing maternal and infant morbidity and mortality. 22. All food-grade salt used in households and food processing should be fortified with iodine to prevent and control iodine deficiency disorders in populations. 23. Fortification of maize flour and cornmeal with iron is recommended to prevent iron deficiency, particularly in vulnerable groups such as children and women. Fortification with folic acid is also recommended to reduce the risk of neural tube defects. 24. Counseling on healthy eating and physical activity during pregnancy is recommended to prevent excessive weight gain and maintain maternal health. 25. In undernourished populations, nutrition education on increasing daily energy and protein intake is recommended for pregnant women to reduce the risk of low-birth-weight neonates. Balanced energy and protein dietary supplementation is also recommended to reduce the risk of stillbirths and small-for-gestational-age neonates. High-protein supplementation, however, is not recommended. 26. Daily iron and folic acid supplementation is recommended for pregnant women to prevent maternal anemia, puerperal sepsis, low birth weight, and preterm birth. If daily iron is not acceptable due to side effects, weekly supplementation may be considered. 27. At the population level, red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age should be above 400 ng/mL (906 nmol/L) to achieve the greatest reduction in neural tube defects (NTDs). However, this threshold cannot predict individual risk and is only useful at the population level. Microbiological assay is recommended as the most reliable method for measuring red blood cell folate concentrations across countries.
